transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

The things that used to mean everything to me—my garden, my quilts, my walks—don’t matter anymore, and I can’t make myself care about any of it. I just feel completely empty, and I don't know how to find the spark to do anything anymore.
How long have you been feeling this way? Has it been going on for at least two weeks or longer?

Oh, it has been much longer than just two weeks. These heavy feelings started shortly after my sister passed away, and it has been going on almost constantly for well over a year now—about a year and five months. I just can't seem to shake this darkness.
Have your symptoms been present nearly every day for most of the day, and have they been continuously present for this entire two-year period without significant breaks?

Yes, I've felt this heavy sadness nearly every day, but it has been about a year and a half since my sister died rather than a full two years. While the deep depression has been almost constant, there was a brief spell last fall when my mood felt a little more neutral. But even during that break, the voices and the feeling of being watched never stopped.
You mentioned voices and feeling watched—can you tell me more about those experiences? Are the voices something you hear even when no one is around?

Yes, at night when the house is quiet, I clearly hear my late sister calling my name from the hallway, telling me I'm a burden and should "come with her." I also know that some of the ladies from my church are working with the hospital and the city to watch me and take my house away. It is very frightening, and I know they are talking about me behind my back.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F33.1", "F20.0"], but based on this conversation, F33.1 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder, Current Episode Moderate) is no longer likely because the patient reports persistent psychotic symptoms—specifically auditory hallucinations (hearing her deceased sister's voice) and delusional beliefs (being watched and conspired against by church members)—that are present even during periods when her mood improved. These psychotic features are not typical of major depressive disorder without a history of schizophrenia-spectrum disorder, especially when they persist independently of mood episodes. The chronicity of symptoms, presence of hallucinations, and delusions that are well-organized and paranoid in nature strongly support F20.0 (Schizophrenia) as the primary diagnosis. The depressive symptoms may co-occur but are better explained as part of the negative or affective symptoms of schizophrenia.

Dysthymia (F34.1) is also a candidate due to the chronic sense of emptiness, though duration has not yet been confirmed. No other diagnostic categories (e.g., psychotic, bipolar, or anxiety disorders) are currently supported by the history.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a prolonged major depressive episode accompanied by persistent delusions and auditory hallucinations, particularly related to persecution and a bereavement context, meeting criteria for paranoid schizophrenia (F20.0). The psychotic symptoms are not limited to the mood episode and have persisted beyond any potential brief mood elevation, supporting a schizophrenia spectrum disorder rather than a depressive disorder with psychotic features.
